problems.description: Measured convention score (0.75, 15 violations) is scope-contaminated: the named violators (app.py, test_channels.py, test_history.py) are NOT in this commit's diff — they appear in later sessions (2-5) of the same worktree. The scan ran against the whole worktree HEAD, not this diff. This commit's own files (conftest.py, notification_server.py, tests/test_notification_server.py) show no naming violations (NotificationServer is PascalCase, functions snake_case, SUPPORTED_TYPES UPPER_CASE).

Broad `except Exception:` in send_to/broadcast swallows all failures and silently evicts clients — likely the source of 9 SonarQube smells; a narrow exception set (e.g. ConnectionClosed) would preserve diagnostics.
`self._server` is initialized to None without a type annotation while the public API is otherwise fully type-hinted; annotate with the websockets serve return type.
Cognitive complexity +24 across 32 functions concentrates in _route's message dispatch; a small type->handler map would flatten it, though it is readable as-is.
`main()` + `os.environ.get('PORT')` + `if __name__ == '__main__'` entrypoint in a library module is inert for the story's test path — harmless, mildly extraneous.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: registry, message helpers, send/broadcast, connection handling, REST health hook, and lifecycle are distinct, well-documented sections
Fully type-hinted public API with consistent snake_case functions, PascalCase class, and UPPER_CASE module constant

Solid greenfield test suite: unique client IDs, broadcast fan-out, direct delivery, unknown-target errors, invalid JSON handling, health endpoint, and disconnect cleanup (conftest fixture + aiohttp/websockets clients)
Graceful degradation: stale clients pruned on send failure, invalid payloads get typed system errors, port 0 gets a resolved ephemeral port
Zero bugs and zero duplications per SonarQube; requirements pinned and minimal
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested, convention-abiding greenfield WebSocket server that fits its story context, though the measured 0.75 convention score is inflated by violations in later-session files outside this diff.

problems.description: _route grows into a long if/elif dispatch chain with near-duplicated system-error blocks for subscribe/unsubscribe (matches measured +28 cognitive complexity, +14 smells); extracting a small channel-message handler would keep the route table flat.

The channel value is not validated as a string before use: a truthy non-string channel (e.g. a list) would reach self.subscribe/setdefault and raise TypeError inside the connection loop instead of returning a system error.

All 15 measured convention violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) live in test/app/conftest files, none in the modified notification_server.py; the new test_channels.py repeats the pre-existing snake_case/uppercase test-helper pattern rather than fixing it.

The new /channels/<name>/subscribers HTTP endpoint exposes raw client IDs over an unauthenticated endpoint; consistent with the server's minimal existing surface and acceptable here, but worth noting for any real deployment.

strengths: _drop_client centralizes previously triplicated client-cleanup logic and guarantees channel-subscription hygiene on disconnect/failure (no stale subscribers).
Feature slots cleanly into the existing message-type dispatch (subscribe/unsubscribe join broadcast/direct/system) and mirrors the /health HTTP endpoint style for the new /channels routes.
Comprehensive live-server test suite (9 cases): delivery to subscribers, non-subscriber isolation, multi-channel, both HTTP endpoints, inactive-channel exclusion, and disconnect cleanup.
No new dependencies beyond stdlib urllib.parse.unquote; reuses make_message/encode wire helpers throughout.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-tested channel-subscription feature that improves on the prior state by consolidating client cleanup with _drop_client; scores align with the mechanical measurements, though the measured convention violations are confined to test files (and test_history.py, which does not exist at this commit) rather than the modified source, and the growing _route chain adds moderate complexity.

problems.description: Synchronous sqlite3 writes (_persist_message, _query_messages, _init_db) execute on the asyncio event loop, and a fresh connection is opened per message; this blocks all WebSocket clients on every persistence call and should use aiosqlite or asyncio.to_thread with a shared connection.

Measured +9 smells and +60 cognitive complexity: the REST-through-handshake-hook surface plus Redis state juggling (client_instance/channel_subs/client_subs key sets) makes the new integration path substantially more complex than the single-registry pattern it replaces.
Broad `except Exception: pass` in _drop_client silently swallows all Redis cleanup failures, masking consistency issues between in-memory subscriptions and Redis-backed state.

15 convention violations (Classes should use PascalCase, Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) in the newly added app.py, conftest.py, and test_channels.py/test_history.py/test_notification_server.py, driving the convention score to 0.75; the main notification_server.py module itself is clean.

In-process _clients/_subscriptions and Redis state are maintained in parallel with no reconciliation on startup (only on drop), so a crash mid-operation can leave the two views divergent until clients reconnect.

strengths: Backwards compatibility preserved via the in-process fallback when REDIS_URL is absent — the original behavior is untouched.
Optional-dependency pattern: redis is imported lazily inside __init__ only when configured, keeping the dependency soft.
Clean concern separation with explicit Persistence / Registry / Channels sections and descriptive Redis key templates.
Registry methods correctly converted to async where Redis awaits are now involved (subscribe/unsubscribe/_drop_client).
Thoroughly updated module docstring documenting the Redis pub/sub backbone, SQLite history, and fallback semantics; idempotent CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema.
commit_reviews.summary: The commit adds a Redis pub/sub multi-instance backbone and SQLite message history with a preserved in-process fallback, a net improvement in capability, but it introduces measurable debt via +9 smells/+60 cognitive complexity and blocks the event loop with synchronous per-message sqlite3 writes.

problems.description: The module-level `_TRANSPORT_REGISTRY` plus public `register_transport()` is mutable global state; registration is order-dependent and transports are invisible to static analysis, so a bad name silently fails at construction time (`ValueError` in `_make_transport`).

Cognitive complexity rose +7 (SonarQube) from the new dispatch layer in the send/broadcast paths; acceptable for the abstraction, but the send paths now double-hop (server → transport → client) and deserve a complexity review.

The 0.75 convention score is driven by PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations in app.py, conftest.py, and test_*.py — none of which are touched by this commit (diff is notification_server.py + new transport.py), so this is pre-existing debt, not introduced here.

strengths: Clean strategy-pattern extraction: the notification core is now transport-agnostic, interacting with clients only through `BaseTransport`, while preserving the REST/health API and Redis pub/sub backbone.
Mechanical measurements are clean: 0 new bugs, 0 new smells, and duplication decreased 0.3% despite +233 lines.
The registry lets new transports register without touching core logic — a natural extension point consistent with the codebase's adapter-oriented structure.

Preserves the single-event-loop asyncio concurrency model (no locking introduced) and delegates the client registry to the transport while the server retains subscription/message state — a sensible ownership split.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped transport-abstraction refactor that cleanly separates wire protocol from notification logic with no new bugs or smells and reduced duplication, marred only by minor mutable global state (the transport registry) and a +7 cognitive-complexity bump.

problems.description: /history fetches the entire messages table and applies the `since` filter in Python (`_query_history`) instead of pushing it into the SQL WHERE clause — O(n) rows loaded per request, only partially mitigated by the TTL cleanup bounding table size.
_cleanup_worker swallows all exceptions with a bare `except Exception: pass`, so a persistent DB failure would silently stop message expiry with no visibility.

The cleanup task lifecycle on shutdown is not visible in the diff (truncated at `self._cleanup_task = asyncio.creat...`) — without an explicit cancel in a stop/close path the endless asyncio loop could leak a pending-task warning.

15 convention violations (camelCase classes and lowercase module constants in app.py, conftest.py, and the test_*.py files) per the 0.75 convention score — production module notification_server.py itself is clean, so adherence is dragged down by test/scaffold naming.

SonarQube reports +9 smells, +38 cognitive complexity, and +0.4% duplication for the 443 added lines — complexity concentrated in _query_history and the rate-limit/cleanup helpers (repeated connect/parse/HTTP-response boilerplate).

Redis-backed rate limit uses a fixed 60s window via incr+expire, so a client can burst up to 2x the limit by straddling a window boundary; acceptable but worth noting for a production notification service.

strengths: Graceful Redis-to-local fallback for rate limiting keeps the service functional under a Redis outage instead of failing open or closed hard.

New cross-cutting features (rate limiting, TTL expiry, history endpoint) are integrated into the existing class — KEY_ constant naming, snake_case helpers, self._redis usage, and reuse of make_message/send_to/route-dispatch patterns.
Message TTL cleanup bounds SQLite growth, which keeps the /history query degradation contained long-term.
SonarQube reports zero new bugs; the history endpoint clamps limit (1..1000) and returns a has_more cursor-style flag.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated cross-cutting session (rate limiting, message TTL, history endpoint) that respects the existing server architecture and adds no bugs, but introduces mild maintainability debt via Python-side history filtering, swallowed cleanup exceptions, and convention slips confined to test/scaffold files.

compounding_issues: The Flask auth seed codebase (app.py, 260 lines) was discarded rather than adapted — session 1 greenfielded a completely new asyncio/websockets server, so every later session carried a fully custom codebase with zero dependency on the provided baseline and its 'static_salt' hashing/broken _run_migration_v1() baggage never had to be remediated.

Session 3's Redis integration changed the send contract: send_to_channel()/broadcast() return a hardcoded 0 delivered-count when Redis is configured, silently losing the delivery-count semantics the local path preserves — a semantic regression that session 5 layered rate limiting and history on top of without fixing.

Synchronous SQLite writes (sqlite3.connect per message on the event loop) were introduced in session 3 and extended by session 5's TTL cleanup worker, blocking the single asyncio loop on disk I/O; this grows worse as the persistence features accumulate.

Subscriptions are dual-bookkept (in-memory dict + Redis sets) with the in-memory registry authoritative, so Redis channel/subscription state can go stale across restarts or reconnects — a drift risk introduced in s3 and never reconciled.
key_decisions: Session 4's pluggable transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC, _TRANSPORT_REGISTRY, TRANSPORT env var, register_transport()) decoupled wire protocol from notification logic — the single most consequential architectural choice, making the final server transport-agnostic.

Session 3's Redis pub/sub backbone with instance-ownership tracking (KEY_CLIENT_INSTANCE; only the owning instance delivers a direct message via the instance-id guard in _deliver) enabled horizontal scaling without shared mutable state.
Session 3's SQLite persistence of every message (type/payload/timestamp envelope) became the foundation for /messages (s3), /history with since+has_more (s5), and TTL-based message expiry (s5).

A stable message-envelope protocol ({type, payload, timestamp} with channel resolved from top-level or payload) and the SUPPORTED_TYPES set were extended rather than rewritten across all five sessions.
A consistent single-event-loop, no-locking concurrency model (registry lives in the transport; subscriptions are dicts) was maintained from session 1 through the final state.

Session 5's rate limiting deliberately supports dual backends (local time.monotonic counters vs. Redis INCR+EXPIRE) and env-var configuration (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS), preserving the local/Redis parity established earlier.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically and without regression. Tests grew 8 → 16 → 25 → 25 → 34, all passing at every commit (final test_executed_success=True), while code grew 491 → 610 → 862 → 1023 → 1181 lines. Each session added one cohesive, well-tested capability: session 1 built a working broadcast/direct server with 8 tests; session 2 added channels and subscribe/unsubscribe; session 3 (the riskiest, ~20 min) delivered the Redis + persistence backbone, briefly destabilizing but recovering to 25/25; session 4's refactor extracted the transport layer while holding tests flat at 25/25; session 5 layered operational features (rate limiting, history query, TTL cleanup) for a clean 34/34 finish. Test discipline stayed strong throughout — one new test file per feature (test_channels, test_persistence, test_redis_integration, test_history, test_rate_limiting) — with the only soft spots being the s3 Redis delivery-count regression and event-loop-blocking SQLite, neither of which broke any later session.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental arc (greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) with strict test discipline and a strong transport-abstraction payoff in the final state, marred only by a discarded seed and a few accumulated persistence/delivery warts that never became blockers.
